title: Nuclear Chemistry
description: Changes in the nucleus: radioactive decay, fission, fusion, and what radiation does.

entries.name: Nuclear equations and decay types
entries.tagline: How unstable nuclei change, and how to write it down.

sections.text: In a nuclear equation, each nucleus is written with its mass number (protons plus neutrons) at the top and its atomic number at the bottom. Both totals must be equal on the two sides of the arrow.

facts: Alpha (α)
The nucleus emits a helium-4 nucleus. The mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number by 2. ²³⁸U → ²³⁴Th + ⁴He.
Beta-minus (β⁻)
A neutron turns into a proton, releasing an electron and an antineutrino. The mass number stays the same and the atomic number rises by 1. ¹⁴C → ¹⁴N + e⁻.
Positron emission (β⁺)
A proton turns into a neutron, releasing a positron. The atomic number falls by 1.
Electron capture
The nucleus captures an inner electron, turning a proton into a neutron. The atomic number falls by 1.
Gamma (γ)
A high-energy photon released as the nucleus settles to a lower energy state. The mass number and atomic number do not change.

points: Alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper or the outer skin, but they are very damaging if the source is swallowed or inhaled.
Beta particles are stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.
Gamma rays need thick lead or concrete.

quiz.q: What happens to the mass number in alpha decay?
Which type of radiation is the most penetrating?

entries.name: Nuclear stability and binding energy
entries.tagline: Why some nuclei are stable and others are not, and where nuclear energy comes from.

points: For light elements, stable nuclei have about as many neutrons as protons. For heavy ones the ratio rises to about 1.5, because extra neutrons help to hold the repelling protons together.
Nuclei with too many neutrons tend to decay by beta-minus. Those with too few tend to emit positrons or capture electrons.
Every nucleus with more than 82 protons is unstable, and so are technetium and promethium.
Even numbers of protons and neutrons are more stable than odd numbers, and so-called magic numbers (2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126) are especially stable.

sections.text: The mass of a nucleus is a little less than the sum of the masses of its separate protons and neutrons. The difference is the mass defect, and it was released as energy when the nucleus formed. That energy is the binding energy. It is also what you would have to put in to take the nucleus apart.
Helium-4: the mass defect is about 0.0304 u. With 1 u equal to 931.5 MeV, the binding energy is about 28.3 MeV.

sections.h: Why fission and fusion both release energy
sections.text: Binding energy per nucleon is highest near iron-56. Splitting a very heavy nucleus, or joining very light ones, gives nuclei closer to that peak, and the difference is released.

quiz.q: Which element is near the peak of binding energy per nucleon?

entries.name: Half-life and radiometric dating
entries.tagline: Using the steady decay of radioactive atoms as a clock.

sections.text: N₀ is the amount at the start, t is the time, and t½ is the half-life. λ is the decay constant. Radioactive decay is a first-order process.
The becquerel (Bq) is one decay per second. The older curie is 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq.

points: Living things take in carbon, including a tiny, steady fraction of radioactive carbon-14, made in the atmosphere by cosmic rays.
After death no more is taken in, and the carbon-14 decays with a half-life of 5730 years.
Measuring how much is left gives the age. If a sample has 25% of the original carbon-14, two half-lives have passed, so it is about 11 460 years old.
It works up to about 50 000 years. For older rocks, dating uses longer-lived isotopes, such as uranium-238 (half-life 4.47 billion years) decaying to lead-206.

quiz.q: A sample has 25% of its original carbon-14 (half-life 5730 y). How old is it?

entries.name: Nuclear fission
entries.tagline: Splitting heavy nuclei to release energy.

sections.text: In fission, a heavy nucleus, usually uranium-235 or plutonium-239, absorbs a neutron, splits into two smaller nuclei and releases more neutrons and a lot of energy, about 200 MeV per nucleus.
One of many possible ways the nucleus can split.

The released neutrons can split further nuclei. If on average one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another, the reaction keeps going at a steady rate, as in a reactor. If more than one does, it grows explosively. A critical mass is the least amount of fuel that can sustain a chain reaction.

points: Fuel: uranium enriched to about 3–5% uranium-235, compared with 0.7% in natural uranium. Enrichment separates the isotopes, for example by exploiting their small difference in the rate of effusion.
Moderator (water or graphite): slows the neutrons, because slow neutrons are more likely to cause fission.
Control rods (boron or cadmium): absorb neutrons. Pushing them in slows the reaction and pulling them out speeds it up.
Coolant: carries the heat away to make steam that turns a turbine.

sections.text: The products include isotopes that are radioactive for a very long time, which have to be stored securely for thousands of years.

quiz.q: What do control rods in a nuclear reactor do?
quiz.a: Absorb neutrons to slow the reaction

entries.name: Nuclear fusion
entries.tagline: Joining light nuclei, the process that powers the Sun.

sections.text: In fusion, light nuclei combine into a heavier one and release energy, because the product is closer to the peak of binding energy per nucleon.

equations: 4¹H → ⁴He + 2e⁺ + 2ν + 26.7 MeV    (the Sun, in several steps)

sections.text: Nuclei repel each other because they are all positive. To fuse they must collide at enormous speeds, which means temperatures of tens to hundreds of millions of kelvin, where matter is a plasma. In the Sun the great gravity and pressure do the work. On Earth the plasma is held by strong magnetic fields (a tokamak) or compressed by powerful lasers.

points: The fuel (deuterium from seawater, tritium made from lithium) is abundant.
It makes no long-lived high-level waste or greenhouse gases and cannot run away like a fission chain reaction.

In December 2022 a laser experiment at the National Ignition Facility in the United States released more fusion energy than the laser energy delivered to the target for the first time. A working power plant is still far off.

quiz.q: Why does fusion need such high temperatures?
quiz.a: To overcome the repulsion between positive nuclei
wrong: To remove the electrons from the neutrons

entries.name: Uses and safety of radiation
entries.tagline: How radiation is measured, used and guarded against.

sections.text: Ionizing radiation has enough energy to knock electrons off atoms. In living tissue it can damage DNA, which may cause cell death or, years later, cancer.

points: A Geiger counter detects ionizing radiation as clicks.

The gray (Gy) is energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue. The sievert (Sv) is the effective dose, which also accounts for how harmful that type of radiation is. The average person receives about 2.4 mSv a year from natural sources such as radon, rocks, cosmic rays and food.

facts: Medical imaging
Technetium-99m (half-life 6 hours) is injected as a tracer and its gamma rays are imaged. PET scans use fluorine-18 (110 minutes), which emits positrons.
Cancer treatment
Radiation from cobalt-60 or a linear accelerator is aimed at tumors to kill cancer cells.
Smoke detectors
A tiny amount of americium-241 ionizes the air. Smoke interrupts the small current.
Sterilization
Gamma rays kill microbes on medical equipment and some foods.
Tracers in research
Radioactive isotopes of an element let scientists follow it through a plant or a reaction.

sections.text: Reduce the time spent near a source, keep your distance, and use shielding. Dose falls off with the square of the distance.

quiz.q: Which unit measures the effective biological dose of radiation?
